title: Three Reasons Why We Keep Reinventing The Same Learning Technology Every Few Years
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Meyer asks why self-paced, pre-recorded instruction keeps returning as a new product, from 1960s Individually Prescribed Instruction to Khan Academy and flipped classrooms to the Modern Classrooms project. Rather than judge any one tool, he argues the recurrence reveals shared beliefs about education held by media, investors, founders, parents and teachers. He lists them: teaching is expert-to-novice information transfer, quality is the quality of the recording, and other learners get in the way of individual learning. He is careful to say users of these tools need not hold the beliefs. His practical conclusion is that anyone proposing a different kind of ed-tech must understand these beliefs and speak with them, not past them.
points: Self-paced, pre-recorded instruction recurs across decades with little reference to earlier versions.
The recurrence is explained by unspoken beliefs: teaching as information transfer, quality as recording quality, and peers as interference.
These beliefs are held collectively by a broad group and need not be held by any individual user of the tools.
Reformers who want a different ed-tech must engage these beliefs directly in order to persuade.
quotes: I’m coming here today not to judge any particular learning technology, just to wonder why we keep reinventing it every few years, generally without any reference to previous versions. I’m trying to understand why its appeal seems inexhaustible and what that appeal says about popular conceptions of what it means to teach and learn.

But what’s interesting to me about this same technology returning from cold storage every few years is that it reveals a secret. It reveals what a huge group of people—including large subsets of the national media, venture capitalists, startup founders, parents, teachers, administrators, etc—believe about education but don’t often say out loud or even necessarily think about consciously.

Learning is the act of an individual and the presence of other learners with differing traits (existing knowledge, interest, participation styles, etc.) inhibits that learning. Therefore, each learner should learn from the pre-recorded information that is best for them.

You can use, love, and probably even invent these technologies without holding onto any of those beliefs exactly. I’m not describing any one person’s beliefs about education. I’m trying to describe why these particular technologies, all of which share a bunch of common DNA, become very popular every few years.

From that vantage point, I think it’s extremely helpful to understand these enduring beliefs about education, the ones shared by lots of people you’ll need to persuade. Change requires us to speak with those ideas, rather than past them.
